newsitem.title: TAIWAN: First Taiwan ship leaves for direct China sailing.
newsitem.headline: First Taiwan ship leaves for direct China sailing.

text.p: The first Taiwan ship to sail directly to communist China in 48 years left the island's southern Kaohsiung Harbour on Thursday with little fanfare.

"The Uni-Order just left the harbour," a port official said. The Uni-Order, registered in Panama and owned by Taiwan's Uniglory Marine Corp, was scheduled to arrive in China's Xiamen port early on Friday after a 12-hour voyage.

The formal voyage across the Taiwan Strait is the first by a Taiwanese vessel since the Chinese civil war ended in 1949 with the communists in control of the Chinese mainland and the defeated Nationalists in exile on the island of Taiwan.
"I am glad that the sailing across the Taiwan strait finally becomes reality," Uni-Order's captain Yao Ming-fu told reporters before the ship's departure.
"I am very happy to sail to the mainland," Yao added.
But Taiwan officials showed no signs of jubilation.
No officials were at the harbour to witness the departure and no ceremony was held or planned at either Kaohsiung or Xiamen to mark the historic occasion.
On Saturday the China-owned, Saint Vincent-registered Sheng Da ship sailed from Xiamen to Kaohsiung in the first direct voyage across the Taiwan Strait.
Taiwan, which has banned direct links with China since 1949, has agreed to allow limited direct shipping with the mainland under its "offshore transshipment centre" scheme.
Beijing regards the Nationalist-held Taiwan as a renegade province and vows to bring it under China's eventual rule, by force if necessary.
Under the scheme, mainland cargoes are not allowed to enter Taiwan customs but can be transshipped at Kaohsiung for onward passage to third countries.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes at Kaohsiung cannot be loaded on ships planning to cross directly to the Chinese mainland.

As well as Uniglory, five other Taiwan shippers -- Yangming Marine Transport Corp, Wan Hai Lines, Nantai Line, Chinese Maritime Transport Ltd and Kien Hung Shipping -- also obtained permission from Beijing to launch the cross-strait shipping.
Analysts estimate that Xiamen and Fuzhou ports have a combined cargo capacity of only 100,000 20-foot equivalent units (TEU) -- tiny compared with the annual five million TEU handled by Kaohsiung.

Taiwan's private companies, which have invested more than US$30 billion in China since a political thaw began in the 1980s, have pressed Taipei to completely lift the ban, saying direct links would benefit the island's economy.
Taiwan has said warmer Taipei-Beijing relations were needed before direct shipping, aviation and other links could begin.
